summary: A first-person narrator in San Francisco describes stopping at a shop near 16th and Mission to check on an Emma Goldman poster, and notices how quickly internet memes and the slogan "DON'T TRUST ANYONE OVER 25" turn into merchandise sold in local stores. At school, the slogan is written on the blackboard in Ms Galvez's Social Studies class, and she uses it to open a lesson on the sixties, the civil rights movement, and the Berkeley student protests. The excerpt is cut off mid-passage.
one_line: A San Francisco teen notes how fast memes become merch, then Ms Galvez's Social Studies class links the slogan "DON'T TRUST ANYONE OVER 25" to 1960s activism.
key_facts: The narrator intended to get one of the Emma Goldman posters and detoured to 16th and Mission on the way to an unnamed destination.
The store at 16th and Mission was shut, but the narrator read its hours off the door and confirmed the Emma Goldman poster was still up.
Half the shops in the neighborhood had DON'T TRUST ANYONE OVER 25 merchandise in their windows, including lunchboxes, babydoll tees, pencil-boxes, and trucker hats.
The narrator says stores have gotten faster at turning internet memes into merchandise, as new memes sweep the net in a day or two.
A video of a guy launching himself with jet-packs made of carbonated water would reach inboxes on Monday, and by Tuesday t-shirts with stills from it could be bought.
Distressed designer jeans carried the slogan written in what looked like careful high school ball-point ink.
The slogan DON'T TRUST ANYONE OVER 25 was written on the blackboard when the narrator arrived at Ms Galvez's Social Studies class.
Ms Galvez patted her hair, set down her SchoolBook, powered it up, and picked up chalk before turning to face the board.
Ms Galvez joked that "Inflation has hit the nation's slogan-writers, it seems" and asked the class where the phrase came from.
A student answered "Hippies?" and Ms Galvez said hippies were the right general answer but that the clothes and music were incidental to the sixties' main importance.
Ms Galvez said California was one of the main places where civil rights leaders came from and was more political than the rest of the country.
Ms Galvez noted that black people in California had been able to get the same union factory jobs as white people, so they were somewhat better off than their cousins in the South.
Ms Galvez said white and black kids rode buses into the South to sign up black voters and protest official state racism.
The excerpt ends with Ms Galvez beginning to describe a steady stream of students from Berkeley.
